newsitem.title: USA: Boeing jets may not fly into Asia air market.
newsitem.headline: Boeing jets may not fly into Asia air market.

text.p: PHOENIX (REUTER) April 18 - Boeing Co champions its new generation of long-range jets as a way for U.S. airlines to tap into the fast-growing Asian market. But some airline executives said demand for those jets will be limited since regulatory restrictions limit access to those countries.

"Even though the new generation of aircraft is welcome, it does not change the lack of access," David Schwarte, managing director of international affairs for AMR Corp's American Airlines, said at the Sixth Annual Phoenix International Aviation Symposium.
Boeing said its new generation of long-range, wide-body aircraft will allow U.S. carriers to fly past the main Asian hub of Tokyo to reach smaller markets throughout the Asian- Pacific region.

"We expect dramatic growth in Asia in the next 20 years. We believe demand is growing vigorously and the 767, 777 and 747 (aircraft models) can serve that market," said Boeing's vice president of business development Dick James.
"With new aircraft, airlines can enter new cities and add new frequencies," James said.
Several airline executives, however, said international politics, not plane technology, controls where carriers fly.
The new Boeing aircraft models "are great pieces of equipment. But it's not enough to have a plane you can fly - you have to have people in it," Schwarte said.

Currently, Northwest Airlines and UAL Corp's United Airlines are the only U.S. carriers with full access to Japan, the most viable Asian hub. Other carriers such as American and Delta Air Lines Inc face restrictions on service to Japan.

The United States and Japan have debated developing a more liberalized aviation treaty to allow more competition, but no new agreement has been reached. The U.S. has "open skies" agreements with three other Asian nations, but those markets have only a fraction of traffic volume that Japan does.
"Japan is so enormous a market that having access to other markets dosen't really help you," Schwarte said.

"Very few markets behind Tokyo have sufficient demand. Even with new generation aircraft we see only a few new routes being added," said Richard Hirst, senior vice president of corporate affairs at Northwest Airlines.
Hirst said traffic volume outside Japan is so limited that U.S. carriers may not be able to justify the cost of operating a wide-body jet to those cities.
"In markets beyond Japan, yields will be much lower. There are thin traffic flows and low yields. Those are economics that make it difficult for U.S. carriers to serve Asian markets," Hirst said.

Hirst said Boeing's existing 747 jet already can reach 85 percent of the Asian-Pacific region, so there may be limited demand for new generation, long-range aircraft such as the 777- 200X. The price per seat for the new 777 will be 20 percent to 34 percent more than some 747 models, Hirst said.

Carriers that cannot operate hubs in Japan are not likely to set up hubs in smaller Asian markets since the economics and the traffic volume do not make sense, Hirst said. Instead, carriers that want to serve the Asian-Pacific market will form alliances with Asian carriers that have existing hubs.
More liberal air treaties with Japan -- not new long-range jets -- determines movements into Asian by U.S. carriers, Hirst said.

"Hubs in Japan will be essential to U.S. carriers getting access to Asia. It may be the only means that U.S. carriers can serve Asian markets in the future. U.S. carriers not hubbing in Japan may find it favorable to develop alliances with Asian carriers with other hubs," Hirst said.
